<objective>
Remove the two blanket UPDATE grants that contradict this phase's own doctrine — the one
that makes GDPR consent evidence self-serve (CR-04) and the one that lets an owner move a
venue onto another tenant's billing account (WR-01) — and close the venue value-domain hole
that would hand Phase 4 unsupported language codes as valid data (WR-11).

**As a** restaurant owner, **I want to** know that the record of what I agreed to and when
is held by the platform rather than by my own browser, **so that** the consent evidence is
worth something to both of us.

Purpose: `grant select, update on table public.accounts to authenticated` is column-blind,
and `accounts_owner_all` pins only `owner_user_id` in its `WITH CHECK`. An authenticated
owner can therefore PATCH their own row and set `plan_tier` to anything and NULL out
`terms_accepted_at`. This was reproduced live. It is the exact anti-pattern CLAUDE.md rules
out, it directly violates the D-21 prohibition this phase declared, and it opens the
billing seam for self-escalation the moment a later phase enforces tiers. The same shape on
`venues` lets an owner re-point `account_id` at a victim's account.

Output: migrations `0006` and `0007`, a tightened Zod boundary, an inverted matrix
assertion, and a new venue value-domain suite.
</objective>

   `/opt/homebrew/bin/supabase status` before running any test.

<assumption_delta_decision>
The `assumption-delta` scan reported `detected: true` with two `pluralization` signals —
"no venue's data leaks to another" and "one owner account can hold multiple venues".

**The identity-model question:** does the primary key / identity model still name the right
noun — is the tenant `venue` or `account`?

**Decision: `no-change`.** The tenant identity noun is `venue`, and it still is. Every
tenant-scoped table FKs `venues.id`; every RLS policy resolves through
`private.get_venue_role(venue_id, uid)`; and this phase's verification confirmed
independently that `account_id` participates in **no** authorization decision anywhere.
`accounts` is the billing parent and the consent record, not an authority axis. Many venues
per account was designed in from the first migration (D-15, ACCT-03) rather than
retrofitted, so the plural was never an assumption that could drift.

**What would force a later promote:** the first time an authorization decision resolves
through `account_id` — most plausibly plan-tier enforcement gating a feature — `accounts`
becomes a second authority axis and `get_venue_role` alone stops being sufficient. This
plan's `venues.account_id` immutability trigger is what keeps that future decision safe to
make, because it guarantees the billing parent cannot have been moved underneath it.
</assumption_delta_decision>

<tasks>

<task type="checkpoint:decision" gate="blocking">
  <name>Task 1: Decide the shape of account writes after the blanket UPDATE grant is revoked</name>
  <decision>How should writes to `public.accounts` work once `authenticated` loses its table-wide UPDATE grant?</decision>
  <context>
    The grant is being revoked either way — it makes GDPR consent evidence rewritable by the
    data subject and the plan tier self-serve, both reproduced live. What is being decided is
    what replaces it, and that decision is a one-way door in two directions. Revoking is
    itself a contract change other code and the test suite depend on, undoable only by
    another migration. And if the answer is "ship an RPC now", that RPC's signature becomes a
    published contract every later phase inherits and every later caller binds to.

    Phase 1 needs no client-side account update at all: `ensure_account` is SECURITY DEFINER
    and writes the consent columns itself, and nothing in the product edits an account field.
    `.claude/CLAUDE.md` rules out the column-list variant's cousin explicitly ("a blanket
    UPDATE policy plus app-layer UI restriction is bypassable via direct PostgREST calls" —
    use "a SECURITY DEFINER RPC as the only write path"), and the phase's own doctrine in
    migration 0001 says every write flows through such an RPC.
  </context>
  <options>
    <option id="option-a">
      <name>Revoke UPDATE entirely; add no RPC now (recommended)</name>
      <pros>Smallest possible surface. Matches the phase doctrine and CLAUDE.md exactly. Nothing in Phase 1 breaks, because nothing writes accounts outside `ensure_account`. No published contract is created, so the later phase that genuinely needs owner-editable account fields designs the RPC against a real requirement instead of a guessed one.</pros>
      <cons>The first later phase needing an editable account field must ship a migration plus an RPC before it can start.</cons>
    </option>
    <option id="option-b">
      <name>Revoke UPDATE and ship `public.update_account_profile()` now</name>
      <pros>The replacement write path exists the moment the grant goes, so nothing is ever in a state where accounts cannot be edited at all.</pros>
      <cons>Publishes an RPC signature with no caller. Every later phase inherits it, and changing a live RPC signature is a breaking contract change. It also has to guess which columns are owner-editable, and the only plausible candidates today (`plan_tier`, the consent columns) are precisely the ones that must NOT be.</cons>
    </option>
    <option id="option-c">
      <name>Keep UPDATE but narrow it to a column list excluding `plan_tier`, `terms_accepted_version` and `terms_accepted_at`</name>
      <pros>A genuine Postgres column-level grant, so it is not the row-policy anti-pattern. New columns are not automatically included.</pros>
      <cons>There is no column to put on that list — `accounts` holds nothing else an owner would edit. It also leaves a direct PostgREST write path open on the table that holds the consent record, which is exactly the surface D-21 wants closed, and it diverges from the doctrine every other table in this schema follows.</cons>
    </option>
  </options>
  <read_first>
    - `supabase/migrations/0001_core_tenancy.sql` — the `accounts` table definition, the `accounts_owner_all` policy at lines 191-196, the grant block at lines 370-395 including its comment explaining why there is no INSERT and no DELETE anywhere, and `ensure_account` at lines 240-295.
    - `.claude/CLAUDE.md` section "What NOT to Use" — the row-policy-plus-UI-restriction entry.
    - `.planning/phases/01-multi-tenant-foundation/01-REVIEW.md` section CR-04.
    - `.planning/phases/01-multi-tenant-foundation/01-CONTEXT.md` decisions D-11 and D-21.
  </read_first>
  <acceptance_criteria>
    - The developer has selected exactly one option id, and the selection is recorded verbatim in the plan summary.
    - Task 2 implements the selected option and no other.
  </acceptance_criteria>
  <resume-signal>Select: option-a, option-b, or option-c</resume-signal>
</task>

<threat_model>
## Trust Boundaries

| Boundary | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| browser -> PostgREST `/rest/v1/accounts` | Any authenticated owner can issue a PATCH directly; the grant plus the policy is the entire boundary, and no application code is in the path. |
| browser -> PostgREST `/rest/v1/venues` | Same shape; `WITH CHECK` is keyed on `id`, so it constrains which row may change and not which values may be written. |
| venue form -> `create_venue` | Values crossing into permanent tenant data that Phase 4's translation pipeline will inherit as valid. |

## STRIDE Threat Register

| Threat ID | Category | Component | Severity | Disposition | Mitigation Plan |
|-----------|----------|-----------|----------|-------------|-----------------|
| T-01G-20 | Repudiation | `grant update on public.accounts to authenticated` | critical | mitigate | CR-04: the data subject can rewrite `terms_accepted_version` and NULL `terms_accepted_at`, destroying the GDPR consent evidence `ensure_account` exists to establish. Reproduced live. Task 2 revokes the grant; `ensure_account` keeps working because it is SECURITY DEFINER. Proven closed by inverting the matrix assertion that previously proved the write succeeded — probing `terms_accepted_version` directly, with a service-role re-read confirming the stored value did not move. |
| T-01G-21 | Elevation of Privilege | `accounts.plan_tier` | high | mitigate | The same grant lets an owner set their own plan tier, which becomes self-escalation the moment a later phase enforces tiers. Same revoke; a separate `expectWriteDenied` probe on `plan_tier` pins it. |
| T-01G-22 | Tampering | `venues_owner_all` `WITH CHECK` keyed on `id` | high | mitigate | WR-01: an owner can re-point `venues.account_id` at a victim's account, attaching a venue to someone else's billing root and putting it in the blast radius of that account's deletion cascade. Task 2 adds a BEFORE UPDATE trigger raising on any `account_id` change — stronger than a policy because it also binds `service_role`. Proven by an explicit error assertion plus an unchanged service-role re-read, with an owner name-edit positive control beside it so the trigger's scope is visible. |
| T-01G-23 | Tampering | `venues.enabled_languages`, `venues.country_code` | medium | mitigate | WR-11: neither layer constrains values, so a crafted form post or direct RPC call persists a venue with unsupported codes that Phase 4 inherits as valid data. Task 3 adds a containment CHECK and an ISO regex CHECK plus matching Zod enums, and a drift test pins the two representations to each other. |
| T-01G-24 | Denial of Service | the two new CHECK constraints | medium | mitigate | Both validate existing rows on creation, so a non-conforming seed venue would make the migration fail to apply. Task 3 requires reading `supabase/seed.sql` first and fixing the seed rather than weakening the constraint; Task 4 verifies both constraints exist in the live catalog. |
| T-01G-25 | Denial of Service | revoking the accounts UPDATE grant | medium | mitigate | A revoke that broke a legitimate write path would be a self-inflicted outage. Task 2 adds an explicit case asserting `ensure_account` still succeeds and returns the same account id after the revoke, and `tests/rls/owner-full-access.test.ts` must stay green as the ACCT-07 positive control. |
</threat_model>
